items.reply: This is by design: the spec places --shout before the name (`greet.sh --shout ada`). `greet.sh ada --shout` ignores the trailing argument, the same way the script has always ignored extra arguments. Other flags and argument parsing were out of scope for this change.

finding.proof: bin/greet.sh:9 runs `echo "${line}"`. Under sh (dash, macOS /bin/sh), echo expands backslash escapes, so `sh bin/greet.sh 'a\tb\c'` prints a tab and drops the newline. The base commit printed `hello a\tb\c`.
finding.claim: Switching from printf to echo changes the output for names with backslashes even without --shout, which breaks the spec's 'without --shout nothing changes'.
finding.suggestion: Print the line with `printf '%s\n' "${line}"` instead of `echo "${line}"`.

finding.proof: bin/greet.sh:8 maps only a-z. Under a UTF-8 locale, `sh bin/greet.sh --shout 'josé'` prints `HELLO JOSé`. With the same input, `tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'` gives `JOSÉ`.
finding.claim: `tr a-z A-Z` leaves non-ASCII lowercase letters unchanged, so a shouted name can come out partly lowercase; nothing in the spec limits names to ASCII.
finding.suggestion: Use the POSIX classes: `tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'`. They follow the locale wherever tr supports it, and are no worse than a-z where it does not.

items.reply: Checked: `sh bin/greet.sh --shout` prints `HELLO WORLD`. After the shift, `${1:-world}` falls back to world (safe under set -u), and then the whole line is uppercased.
The commit message is `Add --shout` with no body, and I can't see a typo in it. If you meant something else, please point to it.

noticed.text: The thread d-reply is the author's own account (point 2 will be changed, points 1 and 3 are declined). It was read as context, not judged.
The only test covers the plain greeting. None covers --shout, --shout with no name, or a name with a backslash.
